title: Innovation in Teams Starts With Noticing Friction
summary: Most team innovation starts with someone noticing friction. How safety, slack time, user context, small experiments and clear constraints help good ideas ship.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Say three people are waiting for the office coffee machine. Linh from support mentions she answered the same customer question eleven times this week. A backend engineer says the logs probably show it coming, since those customers always hit the same error page first. Nobody's pitching anything. Two weeks later there's a small in-app hint that answers the question before anyone opens a ticket.

That's what most useful innovation in a team looks like. No hackathon stage, no big reveal. Someone notices a bit of friction and says it out loud, somewhere it feels safe to share half an idea. This post covers the conditions that make that happen more often: safety, some slack, closeness to users, small experiments, a codebase you can change, clear constraints and the nerve to say no to most ideas.

Start by noticing friction

The teams that keep improving aren't always the ones with the boldest ideas. They tend to be the ones that stay a little annoyed by everyday friction instead of getting used to it. Things worth noticing:

  • A manual step someone repeats every release.
  • A customer complaint support can answer from memory.
  • A dashboard nobody opens anymore.
  • A deploy checklist that takes longer than the deploy.
  • A new hire asking "why do we do it this way?" and nobody knowing.

Each one is a small idea waiting for someone to pick it up. Whether anyone does depends mostly on the team around them.

Make half-finished ideas safe to say

Early ideas are fragile. They sound naive, incomplete or too small. If every suggestion gets cross-examined on the spot, people learn to bring only polished proposals, and the early signal disappears. Amy Edmondson's study of 51 work teams found that teams who felt safe taking interpersonal risks showed more learning behavior, and she counts experimenting in that behavior next to asking questions, seeking feedback and discussing errors (Edmondson, 1999). For how everyday kindness builds that kind of safety, see Kind Engineers Still Say the Hard Thing.

Safety doesn't mean every idea gets a yes. Edmondson is explicit that psychological safety isn't "a careless sense of permissiveness." An idea gets a fair hearing before anyone judges it, and three questions do most of the work: what problem does this solve, what's the smallest test, and what happens if it goes wrong? Curiosity and discipline fit in the same conversation.

DORA, the long-running research program on software delivery, uses Ron Westrum's model of organizational culture. In the "generative" type, failure leads to inquiry and novelty gets implemented, and DORA reports that a high-trust, generative culture predicts software delivery and organizational performance (DORA, generative organizational culture).

Leave some slack in the week

A team booked solid has no room to think. Every hour is already promised to delivery, incidents, meetings and follow-ups, so improvement happens late at night or not at all. DORA names this as a common pitfall: not giving technical staff the time or opportunity to design and run experiments in quick and easy ways (DORA, team experimentation).

The fix can be small. A protected half-day every other week, or one improvement ticket in every sprint that nobody is allowed to bump, lets the team act while the pain is still fresh. DORA also suggests holding regular hackathons. A once-a-year innovation day is fun, but by then most of the year's friction has been forgotten or worked around.

Get close to the people who use it

A lot of good engineering ideas come from touching the real workflow: reading support tickets, watching a customer use the feature, sitting in on a sales call, tracing a failed signup, or spending an afternoon next to the ops team. DORA's advice here is direct: let developers and operators talk to and observe customers. Without that context you get clever solutions looking for a problem. With it, even a modest change removes real pain.

Test small before you pitch big

Small experiments keep everyone honest. Instead of asking the whole org to believe in a big proposal, build a rough prototype, run a new internal workflow for one week, automate one painful step, or measure one number before and after. The idea gets room to breathe, and nobody has to bet heavily before learning anything.

This works best when the team can start without asking. DORA lists exactly that as part of team experimentation: the ability to work on new ideas independently, without permission from outside the team, and to change specifications during development. If every experiment needs three sign-offs, people stop proposing them.

Before you build it

Write three lines: the problem, the smallest test, and the result that would make you stop. If you can't fill in the third line yet, keep thinking before you start building.

Keep the codebase easy to change

Technical quality sounds less fun than innovation, and it's what lets a new idea travel. If every change is slow, risky and expensive, nobody tries anything. DORA's page on loosely coupled teams describes the target: teams that can change their system's design without permission from outside, run most tests on demand without a shared integration environment, and deploy independently of the services they depend on. DORA counts that kind of structure among the predictors of continuous delivery (DORA, loosely coupled teams).

Clear module boundaries, tests you trust, observability that answers real questions and a boring deploy path are the floor new ideas stand on. Without them, a two-day prototype turns into a two-week rescue.

Give clear constraints

Leads help most by making constraints visible. "Two weeks, no new vendor, no schema change, and the first version only needs to help support" sounds tight, and it sharpens thinking. "Be creative!" with no limits can be harder, because nobody knows which kind of idea would actually help.

Research points to a middle ground. A 2019 review in the Journal of Management pulled together work from strategy, entrepreneurship, operations, organizational behavior and marketing. Its model suggests an inverted U: some constraint helps creativity and innovation, and past a point more constraint starts to hurt (Acar, Tarakci and van Knippenberg, 2019). Keep the constraints that shrink the problem and drop the ones that only add paperwork.

Say no to most ideas, kindly

The hardest part is choosing. A team that says yes to every idea finishes none of them and stops trusting its own process. Every idea deserves a clear status, a reason and a thank-you to whoever raised it:

DecisionWhen it fitsWhat you might say
Try it nowSmall, cheap, and the problem is real and visible"Let's run it for a week and check the numbers on Friday."
Park itGood idea, wrong moment"It's in the backlog with your notes. Let's look again after the release."
Wait for the platformNeeds a migration or system change first"This depends on the new auth service. I'll ping you when it lands."
Drop itDoesn't solve a problem we have right now"Thanks for writing it up. Here's why we're not doing it this quarter."

A clear no protects energy for the few ideas that deserve real attention. It also shows people their suggestions get read and decided, which is what keeps the suggestions coming.

Try this week

  • Ask a support or ops teammate which question they answered most this week.
  • Pick one repeated manual step and time it.
  • Next time someone floats a half-idea, ask "what's the smallest test?" before anything else.
  • Put one small improvement ticket in the next sprint and protect it.
  • Go through your idea backlog and give each item a status: try, park, wait or drop.

faqs.q: How do you foster innovation in an engineering team?
faqs.a: Make it safe to share half-finished ideas, leave time in each sprint for small experiments, keep engineers close to users, keep the codebase easy to change and give clear constraints. Most useful ideas start as someone noticing friction in ordinary work and saying so.

faqs.q: Does psychological safety mean accepting every idea?
faqs.a: No. Amy Edmondson, who defined team psychological safety, says it isn't a careless sense of permissiveness. Every idea gets a fair hearing (what problem it solves, what the smallest test is, what the risk is), and many will still be parked or dropped.

Not necessarily. A 2019 review in the Journal of Management by Acar, Tarakci and van Knippenberg suggests an inverted U: some constraint helps creativity and innovation, and too much starts to hurt. A short time box and one clear first user often sharpen an idea.

faqs.q: What does DORA say about team experimentation?
faqs.a: DORA describes it as teams being able to work on new ideas independently, without permission from outside the team, and to change specifications during development. It names not giving engineers time to design and run experiments as a common pitfall, and suggests letting developers talk to and observe customers.
